The word ribbing (noun) has two main, separate meanings. They look and sound the same but refer to completely different things.

This is the most commonly used meaning in everyday conversation.

When someone ribs you, they tease you — but in a warm, playful, good-natured way. It is never meant to be cruel or hurtful. Think of it as the kind of teasing that happens between close friends or family members who are comfortable enough with each other to joke around.

Ribbing, then, is that act of friendly, light-hearted teasing.

Examples:

  • "His teammates gave him a lot of ribbing about missing the penalty kick."
  • "She took the ribbing from her siblings in good humor."
  • "There was plenty of ribbing at the dinner table when he burned the toast."

Key things to understand about this meaning:

  • It is always light-hearted, never mean-spirited. The moment it becomes cruel or hurtful, it stops being "ribbing."
  • The person being ribbed usually knows it's a joke and laughs along.
  • It often happens in groups — at the workplace, among friends, in a sports team, in a family — wherever people know each other well.
  • Common phrases: "take some ribbing," "give someone ribbing," "good-natured ribbing."
  • You can also say someone "ribs" another person (verb), and the act of doing so is the ribbing (noun).
Meaning 2: A Pattern or Framework of Raised Ridges

This meaning is more physical and visual. It refers to a series of raised, parallel ridges — shaped somewhat like ribs in the human body — that appear either as a decorative/functional pattern on a surface, or as a structural framework inside an object.

Think of the bones in your chest — your ribs run in neat, parallel rows and provide structure and support. Ribbing borrows that image.

This meaning shows up in a few different contexts:

a) In Knitting and Fabric

Ribbing is a very common textile pattern where the fabric alternates between raised columns and sunken columns, creating stretchy, ridged strips. You've almost certainly seen this — it's the stretchy, ridged band at the cuffs of a sweater, the ankle of a sock, or the waistband of a hoodie. That band is the ribbing.

  • It stretches and then springs back into shape, which is why it's used at openings of garments.
  • Example: "The sweater had ribbing at the neck and wrists."

b) In Structures (Boats, Umbrellas, Buildings, etc.)

Ribbing can also refer to the internal skeleton or framework of ribs — the structural "bones" — that give an object its shape and strength from the inside.

  • Inside a traditional wooden boat, there are curved wooden supports called ribs running along the inside of the hull. Together, they form the ribbing of the boat.
  • An umbrella has thin metal rods fanning out from the center. Those rods are the ribbing — they are what hold the canopy open.
  • In architecture, a vaulted ceiling (like in a cathedral) often has decorative and structural arched bands crossing it. Those arched bands are the ribbing of the vault.

Examples:

  • "The ribbing of the old fishing boat was made of oak."
  • "She could see the ribbing of the umbrella through the thin fabric."
  • "The cathedral ceiling's ribbing soared up into elegant arches."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

The context will almost always make it obvious:

  • If someone is talking about people interacting, joking, or teasing → Meaning 1 (friendly teasing).
  • If someone is talking about fabric, clothing, structures, or physical objects → Meaning 2 (ridged pattern or framework).

Meaning 1Friendly, playful teasing — the kind that makes people laugh rather than cry.
Meaning 2A series of raised ridges on fabric, OR a framework of rib-like supports inside a structure.

There you have it — the word ribbing fully unpacked, in both its everyday and more technical uses.
